title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to evaluate conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. The preregistered design (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) specified 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded), a single hosted LLM (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"), and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated deterministically and shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and, consequently, no guarded exclusions or replacements were applied. All 150 baseline and 150 guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150; guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, archived execution facts—synthetic provenance and shared generation semantics—mechanistically explain the degenerate null outcome and materially limit inference about contamination prevalence in external, web‑sourced benchmarks. We reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, report deterministic reconciliation and validator traces, explain why the audit was insensitive to generation‑level contamination under the chosen execution semantics, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations to increase audit sensitivity in future studies.

sections.introduction:
LLMs are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated repair. Operational adoption depends not only on model capability but on trustworthy evaluation: measured accuracy must reflect real ability rather than leakage from benchmark items appearing in model training corpora (dataset contamination) or trivial, templated prompts that fail to represent operational difficulty. Recent surveys and benchmark studies emphasize contamination and construct‑validity risks and recommend contamination‑aware audits and verifier‑backed oracles.

We preregistered and executed a confirmatory audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) to answer the following research question: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? Our contributions are (1) a fully preregistered confirmatory experiment executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains why the run produced a degenerate null and prescribes artifact‑grounded audit design changes to increase sensitivity.

Scope and bounded claims. The study targeted a methodological question about preregistered contamination controls under a specific execution regime. The executed sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by a deterministic generator and used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). Those execution facts are archived and restrict inference: the observed zero‑flag, zero‑difference outcome applies to this synthetic sampling and generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑driven configuration and repair. Recent system and benchmark work shows LLMs can produce configuration artifacts and plausible repairs under constrained settings, and that integrating formal verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality [https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.06212, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.22092]. These works highlight both promise and per‑case regressions, motivating verifier‑backed oracles.

Formal verification and oracles. Header Space Analysis and related localized verification approaches provide deterministic checks for reachability and policy properties and are practical oracles for generate–validate pipelines in NetOps research [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.300.8659, https://openalex.org/W2742515467]. Using such oracles reduces false positives from syntactically plausible but functionally incorrect outputs.

Evaluation validity and contamination. Surveys of LLM evaluation emphasize hallucination, benchmark construct invalidity, and dataset contamination risks; they recommend contamination detection, provenance checks, and reporting standards for trustworthy benchmarking [https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660]. Our study implements a conservative, preregistered subset of these defenses and tests their effect in a reproducible execution contract.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. We preregistered the study (contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs. The prespecified confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) per the archived analysis executor.

Detectors and guarded policy (preregistered). The detectors were: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (sensitivity thresholds at 0.65 and 0.50); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to model training cutoffs. The guarded policy deterministically excludes only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80) and replaces them with deterministic retemplated + topology‑augmented items from the same generator distribution, subject to an embedding‑similarity acceptance constraint. These rules and replacement semantics are archived.

Sampling, generation semantics, and implementation choices. The preregistration allowed deterministic task generators for reproducibility and permitted shared generation semantics. For this execution the deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for the confirmatory sample. Execution settings specified independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate): when no high‑confidence exclusions are triggered a single shared model generation per item serves both baseline and guarded episodes. The verification oracle is deterministic_netops_validator_v5, which performs parse→state→property checks and returns a binary pass/fail plus detailed traces. The scoring rule for intent→configuration tasks is full_intent_constraint_validation (validator must confirm intended final state and workflow constraints). All configuration and manifest artifacts are archived (execution/* paths).

Planned analysis and sensitivity. The primary confirmatory analysis was the paired McNemar test with paired bootstrap CI. Prespecified sensitivities included: (a) treating failed calls as failures, (b) testing fuzzy thresholds at 0.50/0.65/0.80, and (c) subgrouping by templated vs realistic items. The preregistration framed power guidance for multi‑model designs; the single‑model plan executed here has reduced sensitivity.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item rather than two independent generations per pair). Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 150 and consistent provider call accounting.

Contamination detector outcomes. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample; the contamination_summary artifact contains no flagged rows. The archived detector logs recorded no replacement operations because the high‑confidence flag rule was never triggered. Importantly, per the archived detector workflow, per‑item fuzzy overlap scores were recorded only when a flag or replacement occurred; since no episodes reached the high‑confidence threshold, there is no archived per‑item overlap distribution to report. The absence of flagged episodes and of overlap aggregates is an explicit archive fact rather than an inferred statistic.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for every baseline episode (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for every guarded episode (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand, paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, equals 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode validator traces and normalized_reference/responses are archived under execution/responses and execution/scoring for verification.

Representative exemplar. A representative archived episode (task-000001) shows identical normalized_reference_answer and normalized_response: "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up". The validator trace for this episode reports parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, observed_touched_field_count = 3, and validation status valid = true. This exemplar illustrates the artifact structure (task manifest → shared generation → validator trace) present in the archive.

Why the paired test was uninformative. Two execution facts—both archived—mechanistically explain the degenerate null outcome. First, sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks; canonicalized exact matches and high fuzzy 5‑gram overlaps against public corpus fingerprints did not arise. Second, independent_condition_generation = false caused a single shared model generation to be reused for both baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions occurred. Together these facts produced identical baseline and guarded outputs per item and made the paired comparison insensitive to generation‑level contamination under this execution.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and limitations of the confirmatory outcome. The archived evidence answers the preregistered methodological question for the executed sampling regime: for provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and conservative deterministic detectors, do preregistered high‑confidence flags arise and do guarded exclusions alter validator pass rates? For this execution the answer is no. This null result is artifact‑grounded and does not generalize to web‑sourced benchmarks, paraphrase‑sensitive leakage, independent re‑generation semantics, other LLM families, or multi‑model designs.

Design lessons and concrete recommendations. Archive‑grounded lessons lead to actionable recommendations for audits that seek sensitivity to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks:
1) Sample provenance‑rich, web‑sourced items rather than provenance‑stable synthetic items so detectors can exercise overlap thresholds against realistic corpora; 2) use independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded conditions are produced by independent calls and cannot collapse to shared outputs; 3) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to amplify cross‑model contamination signals; 4) record per‑item fuzzy overlap scores for all items (not only flagged ones) so overlap distributions can be reported even when flags are rare; 5) add paraphrase‑robust detection (e.g., embedding‑based nearest‑neighbor checks) and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from the archived execution manifest and analysis artifacts documenting the present run's limits.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: prompt sensitivity and shared generation semantics reduced independent variation across conditions; retries and missingness were handled per preregistration and produced no failed calls in this run. Construct validity: our detectors are conservative heuristics and may miss paraphrase leakage; the validator checks only prespecified functional properties and cannot certify production readiness. External validity: single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) and synthetic provenance limit generalization to other models and web‑sourced datasets. Conclusion validity: the single‑model, shared‑generation design reduces statistical power to detect small paired differences; the observed null is therefore uninformative about contamination prevalence in broader settings.

Operational implications. For practitioners and benchmark curators, the principal operational takeaway is procedural: contamination audits intended to detect model‑training leakage must (i) exercise detector sensitivity by sampling web‑sourced items; (ii) generate independent outputs per condition; and (iii) log detector scores for every item. Verifier‑backed validators remain essential oracles for functional correctness but must be paired with auditing designs that can expose contamination signals if present.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We document deterministic reconciliation checks and validator traces in the archived bundle and recommend provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors, and explicit per‑item detector logging to increase audit sensitivity in future studies. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived in the execution bundle for independent verification (see Disclosure Statement).

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
